extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of social psychology / sociology; general educated readers interested in crowd behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the psychological traits, mechanisms, and moral effects that distinguish crowds from isolated individuals, as presented in a classical treatise on crowd behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of unconscious phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The conscious life of the mind is of small importance in comparison with its unconscious life; unconscious motives play a preponderating part in operations of intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern psychology shows that the majority of our acts are outcomes of an unconscious substratum formed mainly by hereditary influences; most daily actions result from hidden motives which escape our observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonality of racial/unconscious characteristics in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious elements that constitute the 'genius of a race' are shared by individuals and in crowds become common property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These shared unconscious qualities make individuals of a race resemble each other and, when pooled in a crowd, lead to a weakening of individuality and the dominance of homogeneous traits over heterogeneous ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weakening/loss of individuality and intellect in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: In the collective mind the intellectual aptitudes of the individuals, and in consequence their individuality, are weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterogeneous elements are swamped by the homogeneous; crowds accumulate 'stupidity' rather than wit—assemblies of specialists can make decisions no better than a gathering of imbeciles because only mediocre common qualities are brought to bear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of new collective characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds create characteristics not possessed by isolated individuals; the crowd's traits are not merely an average but qualitatively new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These new characteristics arise from causes such as the sentiment of invincible power from numbers, contagion, and suggestibility (hypnotic-like effects) that alter individual behavior within the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of invincible power and loss of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual in a crowd acquires, from numerical considerations, a sentiment of invincible power and feels anonymous and irresponsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sense of power lowers restraints; people yield to instincts they would restrain alone, becoming less disposed to check themselves since the crowd is anonymous and in consequence irresponsible (explains readiness for acts like arson or pillage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion of sentiments and acts
rubrics_metrics.description: In a crowd every sentiment and act is contagious; contagion is a hypnotic-order phenomenon that determines crowd behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contagion causes individuals to readily sacrifice personal interest to collective interest; a suggestion spreads by reciprocity and gains strength when common to all, explaining rapid uniform shifts in sentiment and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestibility / hypnotic-like state
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals immersed in a crowd enter a condition resembling hypnosis: they lose conscious personality and obey suggestions that contradict their usual character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological observations show that crowd members may become fascinated, with certain faculties destroyed and others exalted; the suggestion becomes irresistible, especially because identical suggestions strengthen each other by reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automaton-like behavior: loss of will and discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: The disappearance of the conscious personality renders the individual an automaton—no longer guided by his will, dominated by unconscious activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Will and discernment are lost; feelings and thoughts bend in the direction determined by the suggestion, producing impetuosity and acts contrary to the individual's known habits and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descent on the ladder of civilisation in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: By forming part of an organised crowd a cultivated individual may 'descend several rungs' and behave like a barbarian, acting by instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd members display spontaneity, violence, ferocity, enthusiasm, heroism, and susceptibility to words and images that would have no effect on isolated individuals; metaphor: a man in a crowd is a grain of sand stirred by the wind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral variability depending on suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: The morality of crowds varies with the nature of the suggestion; crowds may be criminal or heroic depending on circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds often act unconsciously; examples include heroism in the Crusades and crimes in revolutions—crowd morality may be much lower or much higher than that of the composing individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impulsiveness, mobility, and irritability
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are at the mercy of exterior exciting causes, reflecting incessant variations; their impulses annihilate the feeling of personal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds are slaves to imperious impulses, lacking capacity to dominate reflex actions; this explains quick shifts from bloodthirsty ferocity to extreme generosity, the absence of premeditation, and the short-lived nature of their wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of premeditation and inability to sustain long-term will
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds do not display premeditation; they are incapable of willing or thinking for extended periods, and their sentiments change with immediate excitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds act like leaves in a tempest—animated successively by contrary sentiments—and their mobility makes them hard to govern, especially when public authority falls into their hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappearance of the notion of impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual in a crowd loses the sense of impossibility and is emboldened by the perceived numerical strength to contemplate acts otherwise unthinkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing alone one could not set fire to a palace, the same person in a crowd believes 'number' makes it possible; the certainty of impunity amplifies ferocity when frustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectant attention, suggestibility, and credulity
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are in a state of expectant attention that renders them excessively suggestible and credulous; the first suggestion implants itself and spreads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images evoked are accepted as realities; educated and ignorant alike are equally incapable of observation once in a crowd; this explains the rapid spread of improbable legends and stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective hallucinations and perversion of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds routinely pervert simple events into transformed images and collective hallucinations, confusing subjective images with objective reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sighting of a disabled vessel that was only foliage (Belle Poule), mass spiritualist deceptions observed by reputable witnesses; a single initial illusion becomes the nucleus of contagious perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability of unanimous eyewitness testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The unanimity of numerous witnesses is often one of the worst proofs for establishing a fact; collective observations are frequently erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatises on logic need revision: events observed by many often diverge strongly from reality (examples: battle accounts like Sedan/Waterloo, mistaken identifications of drowned children); indicates low evidentiary value of crowd testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular unreliability of children and impressionable persons as witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Children and highly impressionable persons (often women, children) give recognitions and testimonies that are frequently false or the product of suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial implication: children's statements should be treated cautiously; example: multiple mistaken recognitions of a corpse, later shown to be erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, exaggeration, and absence of doubt in crowd sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd feelings are very simple and very exaggerated: they admit neither doubt nor uncertainty and always go to extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds think in images and are blind to intermediate distinctions; a slight antipathy becomes furious hatred; the absence of responsibility and the sense of power intensify extremes and release envious or ignorant persons from feelings of insignificance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of the educated and the ignorant within crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: From the moment they form part of a crowd the learned man and the ignoramus are equally incapable of observation on matters outside their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social status or prior education offers no protection against collective suggestion; even distinguished observers can be deceived (Davey's experiments, Wallace example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance, dictatorialness, and conservatism of crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds tend toward intolerance, dictatorial attitudes, and conservatism despite momentary revolutionary instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is driven by servility to strong authority and instinctive hostility to changes and progress; though hinted in chapter headings, the text situates these as recurrent crowd traits shaped by suggestions and racial influences.
